title: His Partner Cut the Rope: The Full Case of Joe Simpson
description:
Case 016, the full case file. In June 1985 two British climbers in their twenties, Joe Simpson and Simon Yates, went to the Peruvian Andes to try the unclimbed west face of Siula Grande. A third man, Richard Hawking, who was not a climber, stayed at base camp. They reached the summit on the third day, the first ascent of that face, and started down the north ridge. That night their stove burned the last of its gas, which left them with no way of melting snow to drink. The next morning Simpson fell from an ice cliff on the ridge and broke his right leg at the knee. With nearly 3,000 feet of mountain still below them, Yates knotted their two ropes into one about 300 feet long, dug himself a seat in the snow and lowered Simpson down the mountain a rope-length at a time, on into darkness and a storm. Then he lowered him, without either of them knowing it, over the edge of a cliff. Simpson hung in free space; his hands were frostbitten and he could not climb the rope. Yates, who could not see him, held his weight for more than an hour while his seat in the snow collapsed under him. When he was being pulled off the mountain himself he took a knife from his rucksack and cut the rope. He spent the night in a snow hole, climbed down past the cliff in the morning, found a crevasse at its foot and no sign of Simpson, concluded that he was dead and went back to camp alone. Simpson had fallen into the crevasse and landed on a ledge inside it. He could not climb out past the overhanging ice, so he lowered himself deeper instead, found a slope of snow that led up to a hole and daylight, and then crawled and hopped for three days across the glacier and the moraine with no food and almost no water. He reached camp at night, a few hours before Yates and Hawking were due to leave. It took two days by mule to get him out of the mountains and then to a hospital in Lima. He had lost about a third of his body weight, and his leg needed six operations; two years later he was climbing again. Some climbers blamed Yates for cutting the rope. Simpson always defended him, said he would have done the same, and wrote a book, Touching the Void (1988), partly to set the record straight. Both men have said that cutting the rope is what saved them both. Rook didn't believe it either.

So: would you have cut the rope?

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The mountain, ridge, snow hole, cliff, crevasse, glacier, camp, hospital room, desk and crag in the film are generic low-poly sets, not models of the real places; every person shown is a simple stand-in and nobody's likeness is attempted. The cards on the case board are drawings made for the film, and the book on the book card is a plain invented cover, not the real one. Sources differ on some figures, so the film is careful with them: the summit is given as 6,344 m or 6,356 m (the film gives no height); Yates held the rope for about an hour or about an hour and a half (the film says 'more than an hour'); the crawl took three days or three and a half, and Simpson reached camp four days after the rope was cut (the film says 'three days'); the distance he fell into the crevasse is given as anything from 50 to more than 200 feet (the film gives none). The notes on Rook's board, HE'D HAVE DONE THE SAME and SOME CLIMBERS BLAMED HIM, are Rook's summaries, not quotations.
title_options: His Partner Cut the Rope: The Full Case of Joe Simpson
He Cut the Rope, and It Saved Them Both: The Full Story of Siula Grande
Left for Dead in a Crevasse With a Broken Leg, He Crawled Home in Three Days

experiments.E1_E2: Spine v2 kept from the Short: the cold open is the hang and the slack rope, Rook's doubt is spoken on the lip of the cliff with the drop in frame (no office). The long version then does what the Short had no room for and goes back to the start (June 1985, the face, base camp), runs forward to the cut, and holds back what happened to Simpson until after Yates has walked back to camp alone.
experiments.rehook: 'But here is what he could not see.' at 1 min 57 s of 3 min 17 s (60%): the story the viewer thinks has ended starts again from inside the crevasse.
experiments.hush: Shot 47 (the blade on the rope): the music drops out for 'He cuts the rope.'
experiments.rook_action: He inspects the cut end of the rope on the lip (shots 7 and 8); shakes the empty gas canister by his ear and turns it upside down (shot 23); drops a lump of ice off the ledge to sound the crevasse (shots 58 and 59); reads the chart at the foot of the hospital bed (shot 77).
experiments.rook_mannerisms: Collar pop (9), coin flip (16), hat brim pulled down (36, 94), hat off for the hard beats (27, 48, 49, 51, 67, 75, 93), a feather shed (9, 59), beak tap (85, 87), pocketing the karabiner (94).
experiments.ending: 'Case closed.' in the film; the Short's question (would you have cut the rope?) is kept for the description.

sound_plan.first_frame: One sharp hit at 0.03 s for the rope jerking tight, then wind; no music sting.
sound_plan.music: The engine's score follows the segment moods: hook, tense, calm for the start and base camp, triumph on the summit, tense for the gas, action for the fall, sad for 'nobody is coming', tense through the plan and the lowering, action at the edge, tense for the hold, sad for the cut and the night, wonder for 'Alive', tense in the crevasse, wonder at the daylight, tense for the crawl, triumph at the camp, calm afterwards, sad for the blame, calm, end.
sound_plan.hush: The music is pulled out under shot 47 (the cut).
sound_plan.effects: Axe blows and scrapes for the climbing and the seat, rope creaks for every loaded rope, a heartbeat under the leg and under the hold, ticks for counted things (days, operations, the typewriter), wind on every exposed shot. No effect is placed without a visible cause.
sound_plan.voice: Narration is ducked over the bed by the engine; the rehearsal measured it (see quality_gate).

source_notes: Read for this run on 16 Nov 2026 (every page in `sources` was fetched and read; nothing is taken from memory). Three kinds of source: the climbers' own 1985 expedition report to the Mount Everest Foundation (MEF), the Wikipedia pages on the book, the film, the two men and the mountain (WP), and press pieces and reviews. Could not be read: the Sports Illustrated Vault article (address too long for the fetch tool) and a Red Bull interview (no article text). Every narrated or lettered fact that the Short did not already carry is in at least two of the pages read. June 1985: MEF (summit 7 June, the fall 8 June), h2g2. Both in their twenties: Shropshire Star, Courier, Ebert (exact ages conflict: 25 and 21 in several pieces, but Simpson's birth date on WP makes him 24, and the Spectator says both 'not much over 23', so no ages are given). West face never climbed, first ascent: WP Siula Grande, WP Yates, WP book, MEF, ExplorersWeb, CSMonitor (the mountain itself was first climbed in 1936 by another route, so the film says 'that face', never 'the mountain'). Richard Hawking, not a climber, stayed at base camp: WP book, WP film, Sunday Post, Christian Century, CSMonitor (where they met him is not agreed, so it is left out). Summit on the third day: MEF, CSMonitor, Washington Times. Down the north ridge: WP book, WP Yates, WP Siula Grande, MEF. The last of the gas the night before the accident, so no melted snow to drink: WP book, h2g2, Christian Century, Scholastic. Fell from an ice cliff on the ridge the next morning, right leg, the shin driven up through the knee: WP book, MEF, ExplorersWeb, Spectator, Ebert (how far he fell there is 15 ft to 16 m across sources, so no figure). Nearly 3,000 ft still to descend: WP book, WP Yates, WP film, Spectator say about 3,000 ft was lowered; MEF says about 800 m; hence 'nearly'. Two ropes knotted into one of about 300 ft: WP book (two 150 ft ropes), WP Yates, WP film, Arts Desk, Ebert, Spectator, MEF. An unanchored seat dug in the snow: WP book, MEF, Arts Desk, Spectator. Darkness and storm, lowered over an unseen cliff, hanging free: WP book, WP Simpson, WP Yates, MEF, ExplorersWeb, Ebert. Could not climb the rope with frostbitten hands (and dropped one of his cord loops, shown but not narrated): WP book, MEF, h2g2. How long Yates held: about an hour and a half in WP book, WP Yates, WP film, Sunday Post; about an hour in MEF, Ebert, h2g2; the film says 'more than an hour', which both support. The seat collapsing, being pulled off: WP book, WP Yates, MEF, ExplorersWeb. A knife, taken from his rucksack: Courier, Scholastic (knife: also Shropshire Star, h2g2, IrishCentral; 'penknife' is in one source only and 'Swiss Army knife' in none, so the film says 'a knife'). Night in a snow hole, down in the morning, a crevasse at the foot of the cliff, no sign of Simpson, concluded he was dead, back to camp alone: WP book, WP Yates, MEF, h2g2, ExplorersWeb, Arts Desk (that he called out and got no answer is in one source only and is left out). Lowered himself deeper not knowing what was below: Ebert, IrishCentral, WP book, ExplorersWeb. The crawl: three days in WP book, WP film, Spectator, Sunday Herald, Sunday Post; three and a half in MEF; 'four days later' in WP Yates and the Courier counts from the cut; the film says 'three days'. Camp miles away: five miles (WP book) or six (h2g2), so 'miles'. Reached camp at night, hours before the others were due to leave: WP book, WP film, MEF, ExplorersWeb. Two days by mule, then Lima and hospital: MEF (hired mule for two days to the road, then a truck to Lima, hospital 13 to 22 June), IrishCentral. Lost about a third of his body weight: Scholastic ('a third'), IrishCentral ('over 30 percent'); these are the two weakest sources used, and the film says 'about'. Six operations: WP Simpson, IrishCentral, Washington Times, Scholastic. Climbing again two years later: WP Simpson (1987), Scholastic. Criticised by some climbers: WP Yates, Sunday Herald, Sunday Post, CSMonitor, Washington Times, Christian Century, Courier. Simpson defended him and said he would have done the same: WP Yates, Ebert, Christian Century, Scholastic. The book written partly to set the record straight: WP Yates, Sunday Herald, Washington Times. Published 1988 (book card): WP book, WP Simpson, h2g2. That the cut saved both, as something both men have said: Yates in the Shropshire Star (it saved both their lives); Simpson in ExplorersWeb (the only way either could survive) and the Courier (the cut put him where he could save himself); the film attributes it to them and does not state it as bare fact. Left out because fewer than two pages read support it, or sources conflict: both men's ages, the height of the mountain, any distance for either fall, Simpson standing on his good leg while the knot was passed, following Yates's footprints, the others hearing him call in the night, what doctors told him, the film and the prizes. Staging choices that are not facts: the colours of the two ropes, the axes and clothes, the shape of the snow hole and the stove, Rook's lantern, the mule's blanket and the muleteer, everything in the hospital room except the plaster and the bed, the typewriter and the room he writes in (no page read says how or where he wrote), the crag he climbs two years later, Yates coming down the ice on a rope the morning after (sources say only that he descended), Yates sitting alone on the moraine (a picture for the criticism, which came later, at home), and the time of day of scenes the sources do not time.
